title: Teacher as God, or Only His Good Deeds?
hookLine: one graduation speech says: let your teacher be a god to you. and: follow only our good deeds
carry: the teacher as god, yet follow only the good
tomorrow: a poet dies, and two communities claim him. then what?

cards: Graduation day, the old way. In the Taittiriya Upanishad, students who've lived years in a teacher's home are about to go back into the world. The teacher gives a last speech, and families in India still quote it.
Satyam vada: speak the truth. Practice dharma. Let your mother be a god to you, and your father, your teacher, your guest.
Acharya devo bhava: the teacher, a god. Then, in the same speech, in paraphrase: whatever deeds of ours are good, follow those, and not the others. A god, whose deeds you sort?
Hindu texts argue about the guru, and both sides have scripture. Today, let both speak.

teach.h: DEVOTION TO THE GURU AS TO GOD.
teach.b: The first voice is the last verse of the Shvetashvatara Upanishad. In paraphrase: these teachings shine for the great-souled one who has the highest devotion to God, and the same devotion to the guru as to God.
Here is that side's best case. Some things aren't learned like facts. They pass through trust, the way a young musician learns a raga by giving herself to a master, not by arguing every note.
Some lineages treat the guru as a living doorway to God. This is guru bhakti, and Guru Purnima, the full moon when many Hindus honor their teachers, grows from that love.

teach.h: FOLLOW OUR GOOD DEEDS, NOT THE OTHERS.
teach.b: The second voice is the Taittiriya's teacher himself: follow our good deeds, not the others; and if you're ever in doubt, look to people who are thoughtful, devoted to dharma and not harsh.
That side's best case: even a great teacher is a person, and sorting protects both the student and the teaching.

teach.h: REFLECT, THEN DO AS YOU CHOOSE.
teach.b: The Gita leans in near its end, when Krishna tells Arjuna, in paraphrase: reflect on this fully, then do as you choose. Notice what the Taittiriya does: it says both in one breath.
Many readers hold them that way: deep devotion, kept tied to dharma. Others lean hard one way. The texts leave the argument open, and so does this lesson.

how: Hindu traditions honor the guru deeply, on Guru Purnima and every day, and some lineages treat the guru as a doorway to God; the Taittiriya Upanishad's farewell (speak the truth, let the teacher be a god to you, follow our good deeds) is still quoted to students leaving their teachers.

games.q: what does “modern gurus and their cautions” mean?
o: the vows a guru takes before starting to teach
teachers today, weighed by what old texts ask of them
a list of approved gurus kept by temple councils

games.q: two voices on the guru. tap the pairs.
p: devotion to the guru as to God
follow our good deeds, not the others
let your teacher be a god to you

s: the Upanishads say nothing about devotion to a teacher
the Shvetashvatara's last verse names devotion to the guru as to God.
a teacher in the Taittiriya tells students to follow only his good deeds
whatever deeds of ours are good, follow those, and not the others.
the same Taittiriya speech that says the teacher is a god also says to sort his deeds
acharya devo bhava, and: follow our good deeds, not the others.

games.q: your cousin says devotion to the guru as to God means never sorting a teacher's deeds. you lean the Taittiriya's way. what's the best case for her side?
o: some truths pass through trust, the way a student learns a raga from a master.
there isn't one: no Upanishad asks for devotion to a teacher.
it's easier, since then nobody has to think for themselves.
games.why: The Shvetashvatara ties the teaching to devotion to the guru as to God. A fair argument starts from the other side's best case.

practice: Press your palms together at your chest, the namaste gesture of honor, and hold it for a few breaths. Then let your hands open and rest palms up on your knees, free to receive and free to choose.
Move slowly between the two a few times, and notice that both can belong to one person.

wordCard.voice: Modern gurus and their cautions. Two old answers: devotion to the guru as to God, and follow only the good deeds.

orig.note: Sanskrit: satyam vada, speak the truth; the opening of the Taittiriya teacher's farewell.

carryVoice: Hold onto this: the teacher as god, yet follow only the good. One old speech says both. That closes the block.

sources.ref: Shvetashvatara Upanishad 6.23 (these teachings shine for the great-souled one who has highest devotion to God, and to the guru as to God)

Taittiriya Upanishad 1.11 (speak the truth, practice dharma; let your mother, father, teacher and guest be gods to you; follow those of our deeds that are good, not the others; in doubt, look to the thoughtful, devoted and gentle)
Bhagavad Gita 18.63 (reflect on this fully, then do as you choose)
